Phyllodocidae are sometimes known as paddle-worms owing to
their (usually) large and flattened dorsal cirri. The holopelag-
ic Alciopidae (see Pl. 5h) are previously treated as a separate
taxon in the literature but is here included in Phyllodocidae
as Alciopini. Similarly, we also consider the small and poorly
known holopelagic group Iospilidae (Figs. 24.2a-c) as a junior
synonym of Phyllodocidae and included them herein, a place-
ment supported by molecular data (San Martin et al., 2021;
Rouse, pers. comm.). However, due to their uncertain position
within Phyllodocidae we here refer to them as ‘iospilids’. Benth-
ic Phyllodocidae are common inhabitants in the littoral and the
sublittoral but occur down to the greatest depths (over 8000 m
depth for Sige dogieli) and many have distinct pigmentation pat-
terns; Alciopini is completely transparent except for the very
large and conspicuous eyes. As far as is known, iospilids are also
transparent, though segmental pigment spots may be present on
the antero-dorsal side of the parapodia. Benthic taxa are often
easily recognized by a characteristic combination of a gliding
and sinusoid locomotion. Phyllodocidae vary in size from a few
millimetres in e.g. Nereiphylla pusilla to about a metre in some
Phyllodoce, from 20 or so segments up to about 1000 as in Eulalia
myriacyclum. Especially benthic Phyllodocidae can be spectacular-
ly colourful (e.g, Fig. 24.1¢). Often, there is a garish mixture of
colours and conspicuous segmentally repeated patterns produc-
ing transverse or longitudinal lines on the dorsum, such as in
many Phyllodoce and Eulalia.

The prostomium is usually rounded or elongated anteriorly
and has a dorsal pair of antennae and a ventral pair of palps
(Bigs. 24.1a, b). The palps and antennae are all inarticulate and
similar to each other in all taxa. This has led to a confusing
tradition in the literature to refer to the palps as ‘ventral anten-
nae’. Byes, when present, always occur as a single pair and
lenses are present in most taxa (Pl. 5e-h). In Alciopini they are
complex, extremely developed and cover a large portion of the
head and anterior segments (Pl. 5h). Hermans and Eakin (1974)
described the micro- and ultrastructure of the eyes in Vanadis
tagensis. A median antenna or nuchal papilla may be present
in phyllodocids (Figs. 24.1a, b). In dorsal view the insertion

of the median antenna may be anterior, median, or posteri-
or on the prostomium, whereas the placement of the nuchal
papilla is always posterior. Nuchal organs occur as ciliated pits
(e.g. Eulalia), as ciliated posterior prostomial lobes (c.g. Sige;
Fig. 24.1a), or as distinct, eversible structures (e.g. Phyllodoce,
Chaetoparia). In some taxa such as Nereiphylla, they are fused
with the cirrophores of the cirri of segment 1, and in Noto-
phyllum they form elongated lobes (sce Pleijel, 1991). Nothing
is known about the nuchal organs of iospilids. The peristomi-
um is dorsally invisible and presumably limited to the lips. In
iospilids, the delineation is uncertain between the prostomi-
um, the peristomium, and the anteriormost segments. Cirri
of the anteriormost three segments differ from the following
ones in being long and cirriform instead of the usually flat-
tened shape. Various states of cephalization of segment 1-3 are
present in Phyllodocidae. The first three formulae are modified
from Bergstrém (1914) and that for Alciopini follows Rice (1987):

1+1/1+1/N (e.g, Phyllodoce, Eulalia, Nereiphylla, Chaetoparia,
some Alciopini) \

where ‘1’ refers to dorsal versus ventral modified cirri, ‘N’ to
cirri similar to non-cephalized segments, ‘0’ to absence of cir-
ri, and ‘+’ segment delineation. The ventral cirri of segment 2
often deviate in shape from other anterior cirri in being flattened
rather than cirriform. Note that segment 1 in the Eteone-group
is treated as fully reduced and that the first dorsal and ventral
cirri accordingly are situated on segment 2; however, this reduc-
tion can be questioned and requires further research. In many
taxa (e.g. Phyllodoce, Eumida) segment 1 is dorsally reduced, but
visible laterally at the insertion of the first pair of cirri. In others
(e.g. Paranaitis, Nereiphylla) the anterior segments may be fused.
All segments except the anteriormost ones have (usually)
flattened dorsal and ventral cirri, though the latter are less dis-
tinct (Pl.5e-g). The dorsal cirri are situated on well-delineated
cirrophores. Chaetae and distinct protruding chaetigerous lobes
usually appear from segment 2-4, In some Alciopini, the chaetae
